questions.q: How do you access an item in a list?
options: By its position (index), starting at 0, using square brackets like products[0]
By a name, using curly braces
Lists cannot be accessed by individual item, only as a whole
By its alphabetical position only
questions.explain: Lists are ordered and accessed by index position, with counting starting at 0 — products[0] is the first item, products[-1] is the last.

questions.q: How do you access a value in a dictionary?
options: By its key (name), using square brackets like customer["name"]
By its position, starting at 0
Dictionaries can only be printed in full, never accessed individually
By counting from the end only
questions.explain: Dictionaries pair each value with a named key rather than a position — you look up a value using that key, e.g. customer["region"].

questions.q: What does .append() do to a list?
options: Adds a new item to the end of the list
Removes the first item from the list
Sorts the list alphabetically
Converts the list into a dictionary
questions.explain: products.append("Widget D") adds a new item onto the end of the existing list.

An error, since -1 isn't a valid index
The first item in the list
The total number of items in the list
questions.explain: Negative indexing counts from the end — -1 always refers to the last item, regardless of how long the list is.

questions.q: Why does this lesson matter specifically for learning Pandas later in the course?
options: A Pandas Series behaves like a list with labels, and a DataFrame behaves like a dictionary of lists (one per column) — recognizing these shapes matters even without writing them by hand
Pandas doesn't use lists or dictionaries at all
Lists and dictionaries are only relevant to Power Query, not Pandas
This lesson has no connection to anything covered later in the course
questions.explain: Pandas structures are built out of exactly these two shapes — a Series resembles a labeled list, and a DataFrame resembles a dictionary where each key holds a column's worth of list data.
